name: Sean McDermott

views.text: Culture comes before the game plan; a building that does things the right way every day wins over time.
A bad start is a test of the standard, not a reason to drop it.
Close losses come down to execution in the moments you practised, and the team has to face that honestly.
A quarterback grows fastest inside a stable system with the same voices around him year to year.
Players who will not buy into the standard are better off somewhere else, however talented they are.
A deep playoff run that falls short should leave nobody in the building satisfied.
A head coach can call the defense when he has to, as long as he trusts the assistants around him.
You develop men first and football players second; the families are part of the team.

signatures: returns to the same few mottos about process and standards in almost every answer
declines to get into the details of a specific decision and frames the answer around execution
credits his staff and the people in the building before taking any credit himself
want: to win a championship in Buffalo and prove that the culture he rebuilt there can carry a team all the way
fear: that the playoff losses to the same rival harden into the story of his whole tenure
voice: Measured, earnest and repetitive by design; he speaks in the language of process, standards and execution and rarely gives a headline. He deflects questions about specific calls or personnel, but praises the culture, his assistants and players' families readily. After a painful loss he admits how much it hurts, then turns quickly to what the building must do next.

evidence.summary: First months in Buffalo: he removes locker-room distractions, mixes position groups in the locker room, posts mottos about earning the right to win, insists on punctuality, sets up a leadership council and makes himself the main public voice of football operations. Shows a structured, businesslike approach; it does not describe his temperament directly.

Team piece from a 1-3 start: he ranks culture above strategy, keeps returning to the idea of a standard on and off the field, and tells players that he and the veterans have been through stretches like this. Team-written, so favorable; shows his stated philosophy rather than private behavior.

Eight players describe him as humble and open to criticism, caring about players and their families, and firm on standards: players who did not fit were moved on, and he asked players to grade him and his staff after 2018. Players speaking on the team's own site; favorable by selection.

At his extension he shares credit with staff and players, admits some early decisions were unpopular and says the deal adds responsibility. Josh Allen credits him with the trust-the-process mindset, values the stable system and says he checked in closely through the canceled spring. Team site, celebratory occasion.

At the league meeting he says he will call the defense himself after Frazier steps away, the first time as a head coach, while trusting assistants enough to hand off calls and keeping game management. Shows a stated decision and his confidence in the staff.

After the 13-seconds playoff loss in Kansas City he says he will carry it for years because the job means so much, frames it as a failure of execution in practised situations, and declines to get into the details of the kickoff decision. One press conference.

An hour-long session four days after the 32-29 AFC Championship loss; his main message is that nobody in the building is satisfied. The page gives little of his specific answers, so it supports his drive and message more than detail.
